meta.description: Milton Berle didn't coin it. The saying appears by 1968 and 1976, before the first Berle credit in 1977. Quote Investigator calls it essentially anonymous.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Laughter is an instant vacation'?
meta.ogDescription: Milton Berle didn't coin it. The line predates his 1977 credit by nearly a decade; Quote Investigator calls the origin anonymous.

answer.label: Not originated by Milton Berle — an older, essentially anonymous saying
answer.authorDates: saying attested by 1968; first tied to Berle in 1977
answer.sourceLine: Milton Berle is the name the line is pinned to, but it is not his coinage. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the idea already in print in 1968 — Eugene P. Bertin’s “It is instant vacation” in the Pennsylvania School Journal — and a compact newspaper form credited to Robert Zwickey in 1976, both before the earliest Berle ascription in 1977. QI concludes “anonymous may be the most accurate ascription”; Berle (and later Bob Hope) only helped popularize it.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “It is instant vacation” — Eugene P. Bertin

trail: 1968: Eugene P. Bertin writes that laughter “is instant vacation” in the Pennsylvania School Journal, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1976: a compact newspaper version is credited to Robert Zwickey; the first Milton Berle ascription appears in 1977, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Today the line is routinely sold as pure Berle, e.g. on Goodreads ↗, with no source given.
QI’s verdict: “anonymous may be the most accurate ascription” — Berle and Bob Hope popularized it rather than coined it (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The modern compact wording. Its earliest ancestor is Eugene P. Bertin’s 1968 line that laughter “is instant vacation,” with a tightened newspaper form appearing in 1976 before any tie to Milton Berle.

author.name: Milton Berle
author.heading: Milton Berle — popularizer, not author
author.bio: Milton Berle was a vaudeville-bred American comedian whose Texaco Star Theater made him television’s first breakout star in the late 1940s, earning the nickname “Mr. Television.” A relentless collector and reciter of one-liners, he became a natural magnet for stray witticisms — which is how “Laughter is an instant vacation” came to be pinned to him around 1977, years after the saying was already circulating. He helped popularize it, but the evidence does not show he coined it.

misattribution.heading: How Milton Berle got the credit
misattribution.intro: A feel-good one-liner with no clear author drifted onto a famous funnyman. The paper trail shows the saying circulating before Berle’s name was ever attached.

items.why: The first known tie to Berle is a 1977 optometry-journal column (“I agree with Milton Berle when he says…”), which is nearly a decade after the idea appears in print in 1968, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Hope used the line in a 1985 UPI essay but explicitly disclaimed originality (“It’s been said…”), per Quote Investigator ↗.
Bertin’s 1968 Pennsylvania School Journal line is the earliest match, but QI cautions “the evidence is not strongly compelling,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that no one owns this line: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes “anonymous may be the most accurate ascription.”

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Berle
lead: Milton Berle was, by trade, a joke magnet — famous both for his encyclopedic memory of gags and for a reputation as a borrower of them. A short, warm, quotable line about laughter is exactly the kind of thing that gravitates toward a name like his once it is loose in the culture.
The result is a quote that feels authentically “Berle” while the documentary record shows it moving through school journals and newspaper columns first, picking up his name only afterward.
context.pull: The line reached Berle after 1977 — the idea was already in print by 1968.
